newsitem.title: UK: British abortion rate jumps after birth pill scare.
newsitem.headline: British abortion rate jumps after birth pill scare.

text.p: The number of women having abortions in England and Wales jumped sharply earlier this year after a health scare over contraceptive pills in October 1995, official figures showed on Thursday.

Abortions performed in the first quarter of 1996 rose by 6.7 percent to 42,990, according to the Office for National Statistics. At 3.3 per thousand women, the abortion rate was the highest since the first quarter of 1991.
Family planning experts say many women stopped taking the contraceptive pill due to a scare prompted by health warnings from the Government's Committee on the Safety of Medicines.
The committee said new research showed some low-dose contraceptives could increase the risk of potentially fatal blood clots in the legs.

It announced that seven of the newest and most popular brands of contraceptive pill containing the hormones desogestrel or gestodene carried twice the risk of potentially fatal thrombosis compared with older types of pill.

But the risk was still a very low one, and lower than the risk of thrombosis with pregnancy. Family planning experts said women risked their health more by going off the suspect pills than they would have by staying on them.

The government was criticised at the time for publishing its views on the research without giving Britain's 190,000 family doctors prior warning, and for pre-empting an investigation by a European committee.
